title: Hudhayfah, keeper of secrets
hook: the keeper of secrets, who asked about harm so he could avoid it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Musa, whose recitation the Prophet heard in the night. Your line was: a voice like Dawud's. When did you lower your voice instead of raising it? Day eight hundred sixty.

What brings reward? What is best? Those were the questions people brought to the Prophet. Later, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, a companion, tells his listeners how his own questions ran the other way. People used to ask the Messenger of God about the good, he says. I used to ask him about the evil, because I was afraid it would catch me. Plenty of us collect advice about what to do. Hudhayfah collected warnings. Today: Hudhayfah.
screen: `THEY ASKED ABOUT THE GOOD.` → `HE ASKED ABOUT THE EVIL.` → `AFRAID IT WOULD CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: That sentence opens a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Hudhayfah goes on to describe a conversation with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He asks: we were in ignorance and harm, and God brought us this good. Will there be harm after this good? Yes, the Prophet says. And after that harm, good again? Yes, but with some smoke in it, some haze. The questions keep going, Hudhayfah pressing for the next turn and the next, until he asks the practical one: and if that time reaches me, what do you command me to do? The point of all the asking was not gloom. It was a plan. Find out where the road gets dangerous so you can walk around it. His fellow companions noticed something else about him. In Bukhari, Abu al-Darda refers to Hudhayfah as the one among them who holds the secret that no one else knows. Tradition says the Prophet had told him things he told no one else, including who among the people of Medina were hypocrites, and that Hudhayfah kept it. Some reports say even Umar would ask him, worried, whether his own name was on that list, and that Hudhayfah would only say no to him, and name no one else. Those details come from later reports, not from Bukhari. Put the two together. The man who asked about harm was also the man trusted with hard knowledge, and he didn't spend it on gossip. Knowing where the danger was did not make him suspicious of everyone. It made him careful with himself, and quiet about others: honest about the dark, and discreet with what he knew.
screen: `WILL THERE BE HARM AFTER THIS?` · `GOOD AGAIN, BUT WITH HAZE.` · `WHAT DO YOU COMMAND ME TO DO?` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SECRET.` · then, large: `ASK ABOUT THE HARM.`

segments.voice: The practice: know your own weak spot. Close your eyes if that helps, and breathe slowly. Ask yourself Hudhayfah's question, pointed inward. Where does harm usually catch me? A certain hour of the night. A certain app. A certain conversation that always turns sour. Anger when I'm hungry. Don't scold yourself. Just name it, the way you'd mark a pothole on your street. Breathe in, and see it clearly. Breathe out, and think of one small way to walk around it this week. If you pray, you can ask for protection from it. This one stays between you and God, or you and yourself. The bell holds the time.
Hudhayfah. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, the companion who asked the Prophet about harm so he could avoid it, remembered as the keeper of secrets. Today's word.
Your line: ask about the harm. Today, when you meet the weak spot you named, take the detour you planned, once. Day eight hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Muslims quote Hudhayfah's words about asking of evil in order to avoid it, and scholars cite his long report in Bukhari when discussing how to hold fast during times of trouble.

pairs: asked the Prophet about the good
called him the holder of the secret

myth: Hudhayfah asked about evil because he was fascinated by it
he says he asked because he was afraid it would catch him, and he pressed for what to do.
the Prophet said good would return after harm, but with some haze in it
that's one turn in Hudhayfah's long report in Bukhari.
Hudhayfah spread the secrets he was told

fork.setup: you're Hudhayfah. the Prophet has just told you hard times will come after the good. what do you ask next?
options: if it reaches me, what do you command me to do?
fork.reveal: he asked the practical question: what should I do if I live to see it? the point of his asking was a plan.

original.note: Arabic: the companion's name, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a companion who dwelled on the dark side of things.
what it means: he asked about harm so he could avoid it, and pressed the Prophet for what to do.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's report of good, harm, and good with haze, and Abu al-Darda naming him the holder of the secret.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3606; Sahih Muslim 1847 (Hudhayfah: people asked about good, I asked about evil)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory: confirm Bukhari 3606, Muslim 1847, Bukhari 3742.
The hook frames the report as told to listeners years later (it is narrated through Abu Idris al-Khawlani); no place is named. Confirm.
That the secret concerned the names of the hypocrites, and the Umar anecdote, come from later reports; framed as tradition. Confirm sources.
Year 3 day 783 told Hudhayfah's night mission at the Trench; avoided here.
